cards.title: Lead with facts instead of adjectives for ad and landing copy
cards.summary: Replace vague adjectives and opinions with specific, verifiable facts to make ad copy and product claims carry weight.
cards.use_when: Writing or auditing headline, PDP or ad copy where current claims feel vague ('high quality', 'unequal', 'sloppy') and you need credibility.
steps: Identify every adjective-based claim in the draft (e.g. 'better', 'unequal', 'sloppy', 'premium').
Convert each into a concrete fact, number, comparison or observable detail: instead of 'unequal' show the graph/difference; instead of 'Tiger was sloppy' say 'he averaged 7 fairways vs his usual 11'.

For ecommerce: replace 'our jeans are better made' with a spec (stitch count, denim weight, warranty length, number of returns per 1,000). Replace 'fast shipping' with the actual measured delivery time.
Once rooted in a fact, layer interpretation or momentum on top — the fact earns the right to the claim.
Keep a running 'arsenal' of facts about the product, brand and category so you're never writing from adjectives alone.
caveats: The source treats this as a principle, not a measured benchmark; the golf figures are an analogy, not ecommerce data.
Facts must be true and checkable — fabricated specificity destroys the credibility the technique is meant to create.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: Structure a newsletter with five to six dense examples and built-in conflict
cards.summary: Harry Dry's newsletter formula: five to six concrete examples per issue, each containing conflict, written in short paragraphs.
cards.use_when: Planning an email newsletter, retention email or content send for an ecommerce audience where engagement matters more than list size.
steps: Treat the send as 'more letter than news' — open with a time-and-place personal intro (what you can see out the window, what's happening in your life) rather than a brand announcement.
Include five or six examples/items rather than one long piece; density is the value.
Build conflict into almost every example: use before/after, problem/solution, or 'how everyone else does it vs how this brand does it'.
Write the conflict by hinging on an implicit 'but' rather than repeatedly writing the word 'but' — narrate the turn naturally.
For ecommerce: frame a product story as 'every competitor positions X way; here's how we position it' or 'here was the problem, here's the fix' rather than a flat feature list.
Close with a conclusion so the letter has a shape.
caveats: Source notes engagement, not subscriber count, is the meaningful metric — 100k subscribers at ~50% open was cited as illustrative, not a target.
This is the writer's personal format, presented as his own method, not a universal rule.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: Keep paragraphs to two lines and let each one earn its place
cards.summary: Short paragraphs help distracted readers move through copy, and force sharper self-editing.
cards.use_when: Formatting email, PDP or landing-page body copy that readers will skim on mobile or in a feed.
steps: Cap paragraphs at roughly two lines; the source reports never writing a paragraph longer than two lines in his newsletter since 2021.
Use the three-line test: if a paragraph runs to three lines, you're probably not explaining it clearly — cut words or sentences until it's two.
Treat short paragraphs as stepping stones the reader can 'swing between' when attention is low.
Give strong lines room to breathe by isolating them as their own short paragraph.

Apply a burrito test to each paragraph: pull one sentence out — if it still works without it, the sentence probably didn't belong there. (Kaplan's law of words: words not working for you are working against you.)
caveats: The source explicitly says he isn't claiming short paragraphs are inherently good or bad — it's his idiosyncratic style, chosen for readability and editing discipline.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: Write simply by rewriting, not by trying to write simply the first time
cards.summary: Simplicity comes from repeated rewriting — write several versions of the same line and pick the best pieces.
cards.use_when: Drafting a headline, tagline or hero copy for a PDP or ad and the first pass feels clunky.
steps: Accept that you cannot write simply in the first draft; simplicity is an editing output.
Write a sentence or paragraph, then copy-paste and rewrite it several times, ending with four or five versions of the same line.
Deliberately allow some rewrites to be bad — the freedom to fail produces more original options.
Get better feedback by showing reviewers multiple versions rather than one; a reviewer can say 'use that sentence but put it in that one'.
Reference good writing guides (e.g. Zinsser's On Writing Well, Forsyth's Elements of Eloquence) if you want to go deeper.
For ecommerce: produce 4-5 hero headline variants for the same product page or ad and merge the strongest phrases across them.
caveats: The source says this process 'caused me a lot of turmoil over the years' and is unsure whether to recommend it — it is a personal method, not a guaranteed shortcut.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: Use 'and' as a red flag when scoping a product or brand
cards.summary: The strength of an idea is inversely proportional to its scope — 'and' on a landing page usually signals a diluted offer.
cards.use_when: Writing landing pages, brand taglines or collection descriptions and deciding what the store or product actually stands for.
steps: Scan your landing page or tagline for 'and' joining multiple categories: 'we sell jeans and t-shirts and socks and have dressing rooms'.
Recognise this as a scope problem, not just a copy problem — it signals an unfocused offer.
Narrow to one thing done well, e.g. 'We make jeans. That's it.' The source cites this as Hiut Denim's tagline (worn by supermodels in London, dads in Ohio).
The same principle applies to images: the strongest covers/images are one clean concept (the Velvet Underground banana, Dark Side of the Moon prism) — one image beats seven unrelated ones.
For ecommerce: test whether a one-category message outperforms a multi-category message on the same traffic before broadening the scope.
caveats: Supported by brand examples, not by ecommerce conversion data; treat as a positioning heuristic to test, not a proven rule.
The source does not claim multi-category stores are wrong, only that the strongest ideas are narrow.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: Structure copy by dividing it into named, parallel parts
cards.summary: Structure equals dividing lines plus parallelism — split a big idea into two or three labelled parts readers can hold onto.
cards.use_when: Writing a long-form sales page, PDP story, category page or ad narrative that currently feels like a wall of text.
steps: Take the large idea (e.g. 'copywriting') and divide it into buckets: who are you talking to, what are you saying, how are you saying it.
Use the 'two things that look like one' move: show that what readers think is one thing is actually two (e.g. 'get 100 readers' vs 'get the next 9,900 readers'), and use that as part one/part two.
Apply parallelism so the parts are grammatically and conceptually matched.
For ecommerce: split a product page into parallel, scannable parts (the problem / the product / the proof) rather than a single block of features.
Treat structure as chapters — 17 loose videos are like a book with no chapters; give the reader something cohesive to hold.
caveats: The source cites the 'That's interesting' paper (attributed to 1971) as the origin of the 'show two things are one / one thing is two' framing — treat the citation as his reference, not a verified fact.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: Hold a high quality bar and never let it fall — ship only 9/10 work
cards.summary: Your work is your standards: define what 'good' looks like and refuse to publish anything below it.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether a product page, ad, email or creative is ready to ship, especially under deadline pressure.
steps: Set an explicit bar: the source ships only 'nine out of ten plus' — if it doesn't meet it, it doesn't go out.
Accept that holding the bar will make some people angry, anxious or cause them to stop working with you — the mentor quoted says this is the price.
Define 'good' concretely: take a walk, come back, and ask 'can I take anything away from this?' If nothing can be removed and it reads line-to-line, it's done.
Use the 'worn by supermodels in London, dads in Ohio' test: a line you cannot add to or subtract from and improve is finished.
For ecommerce: apply the same check to hero copy and ad hooks before launch rather than shipping the first acceptable version.
caveats: The line 'you can't add a word to that ad' is the source's subjective standard of quality, not an objective benchmark.
Holding an absolute bar has real costs (slower shipping, friction with collaborators) that the source acknowledges.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: Build conflict into ad creative using the implicit 'but'
cards.summary: Conflict (before/after, problem/solution, us-vs-them) makes messages memorable because humans remember relatively.
cards.use_when: Writing ad hooks, product stories or comparison sections where the copy reads flat and factual.
steps: Identify the implicit 'but' in the story: 'I woke up at 8:52 and started looking for clothes, but my mum ran up the stairs and told me not to do the interview in those shorts.'
Render it naturally — don't literally write 'but this happened, but this happened'.
Use the simplest conflict forms: before/after, here's the problem / here's the solution, here's how everyone else does it / here's how we do it.
Use contrast deliberately: pickle juice makes orange juice taste sweeter — the comparison makes each element memorable.
For ecommerce: frame a product story as 'here's how every other screen recorder positions itself; here's how Loom did it' (positioning conflict) or 'here's what went wrong, here's the fix'.
Human memory is relative, so pairing your product against a real alternative sharpens recall.
caveats: The Loom positioning story is the source's illustrative example of the technique, not a measurable result; the 'worth more than the whole screen recorder bucket combined' claim is his characterization.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: Build a fact arsenal from first-hand experience, not invented detail
cards.summary: Writers like Ogilvy, Bukowski and Plath produced memorable work because they had direct experience of their subject — taste and conviction come from lived observation.
cards.use_when: Deciding what product details, founder stories or category observations to feature in your ad or PDP copy.
steps: Collect two kinds of experience: (1) direct observation — stand in the car, notice the loudest noise at 60 mph (Ogilvy's Rolls-Royce headline came from a motor magazine writer who actually did the drive); (2) long-term expertise — Bukowski worked as a postman for 20 years and wrote Post Office, Plath interned at a New York fashion magazine and wrote a disillusioned intern.
Translate this to ecommerce: actually use the product, talk to customers, note the specific detail a competitor couldn't claim ('loudest thing you can hear is the electric clock').
Look for the specific, concrete observation sitting right in front of you (the hail outside, the green tea, the mess) rather than reaching for generic phrases.
Avoid 'gumming together long strips of words already set in order by somebody else' — that is what the source says predictive AI does.
caveats: The Ogilvy 'increased Rolls-Royce sales by 50%' figure is given as the source's account of a historical ad, not a verified benchmark for you.
Whether these writers' backgrounds 'caused' their work is the source's interpretation, not a proven causal claim.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: Use AI as a tool, but judge output by your taste and conviction
cards.summary: AI can assist research and drafting, but has no taste, no belief and no lived experience — your standards decide whether its output is good.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to use AI in writing PDP copy, ad copy or newsletters without producing generic output.
steps: Treat AI as a research and drafting tool, not an author — the source compares it to the pen-to-typewriter and film-to-digital switches, which didn't make work better on their own.
Before publishing AI-assisted copy, apply the quality bar test: can you subtract anything and improve it? Does it read line-to-line?
Check whether the copy contains genuine belief or conviction — AI 'does not believe something'; a good writer sees something, believes something and writes about it.
Check whether the copy contains specific observation or experience ('AI is predictive — it lays out what has been laid out before').
For ecommerce: use AI for volume variants, then merge and cut using your own judgement; don't ship the first generated version.
The source suggests if you believe AI will do a better job than you, it probably will — so maintain your own standard deliberately.
caveats: The source says the future of AI is unknown and calls it 'a great research tool'; he explicitly does not claim it cannot take your job, only that he doesn't think it can do what he does.
The generative-fill/Abbey Road example is an anecdote about taste, not evidence about AI's current capabilities.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: Protect silence and focus before writing sessions
cards.summary: Starting the day with silence and a walk rather than a feed improves the quality of writing work.
cards.use_when: Scheduling time to write ad copy, product pages or a newsletter that actually needs to be good.
steps: Avoid opening TikTok/Instagram first thing — the source says it makes the day 'drudge' and slow.
Sit in silence, take a walk in the park with no earphones, and collect your thoughts before writing.
In shared writing retreats, the source and the Cultural Tutor agree not to talk until dinner (5 or 6 pm) to preserve intensity.
Apply this to ecommerce teams: block uninterrupted writing time for launch copy and creative rather than writing between meetings.
The source's operating principle is 'silence and action'.
caveats: This is a personal working habit from a solo writer, not a team or agency workflow, and has no controlled evidence behind it.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx
